item.title: Gold edges up in Asia on the energy truce narrative, that looks like a VERY shaky support
item.description:
For gold, the key channel in this conflict has been oil rather than safe-haven demand: escalation has lifted energy prices and Fed hike expectations, pushing up yields and the dollar and weighing on bullion. On that logic, a credible energy truce would be supportive, but this one was disputed within hours and has not been confirmed by Moscow, so a rally built on it rests on weak foundations. A breakdown would likely put Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries back in play, tightening diesel supply and reinforcing the inflation pressure that has hurt gold. Wednesday’s US CPI and Gulf attacks, which move oil far more, are the stronger drivers.

---

Gold’s logic in this war is simple: lower oil helps it, so a truce should too, but not one that was disputed before the day was out.

Summary:

  • Gold edged higher in Asian trade on Monday, with some market chatter attributing the move to Trump’s Russia-Ukraine energy ceasefire
  • Zelenskyy said Russia struck the CHP-5 power plant in Kharkiv and a plant in Kyiv hours after the truce was announced on Sunday
  • The Kremlin has not commented, and neither side appears to have publicly confirmed the terms before Trump’s announcement
  • Ukraine says it will stop striking Russian energy facilities if Russia does the same
  • Previous Trump-brokered energy pauses, in spring 2025 and earlier this year, failed to last
  • US CPI on Wednesday and Fed Chair Warsh’s remarks on Friday are likely to matter more for gold

Gold edged higher in Asian trade on Monday, trading above $4,200 an ounce, with some market chatter crediting the move to Donald Trump’s announcement of an energy ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine. The narrative looks fragile: within hours of the announcement, Kyiv said Russia had struck Ukrainian power plants, and Moscow has yet to say whether it agreed to the truce at all.

Trump announced on Sunday that both sides had agreed to an immediate halt to attacks on energy infrastructure. That evening, Russia struck the CHP-5 thermal power plant in Kharkiv, according to Ukrainian officials, with a local official telling ABC News it was hit at least twice and caught fire. President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said a plant in Kyiv was also targeted, and that Russia had carried out more than 200 strikes on Ukraine’s power generation and transmission over the past week. The Kremlin had not commented at the time of writing, and Ukrainian officials said they learned of the deal from Trump’s social media post.

Zelenskyy said Ukraine supports the truce and would stop striking Russian energy facilities if Russia did the same. Similar arrangements have broken down before: a 30-day moratorium brokered by Trump in spring 2025 did not last, and a week-long pause on strikes against Kyiv’s energy system ended on February 1 this year with renewed attacks.

The link between the truce and gold runs through energy prices rather than safe-haven demand. Throughout the Iran war, escalation has tended to hurt bullion by lifting oil, raising inflation expectations and strengthening the case for further Federal Reserve hikes, which pushes up yields and the dollar. On that logic, a lasting energy truce would be positive for gold by easing fuel prices. The problem is that this truce was disputed within hours, and a Russia-Ukraine energy pause is a much smaller factor for oil than supply from the Gulf.

The pattern was visible last week. Gold rose more than 1% on Thursday as oil fell and the dollar softened after Trump said the US would not attack Iran before the midterm elections. By the same token, weekend attacks on Saudi Arabia, including Houthi claims of strikes on Aramco facilities, are a risk for gold if they push crude higher. Bullion is still around 25% below its January record near $5,600 and has slipped about 2% over the past month.

The bigger tests come later in the week. US consumer price data on Wednesday (preview one, preview two) will shape expectations for an October Fed hike, and Fed Chair Kevin Warsh speaks early on Friday. A firm inflation reading would likely matter far more for gold than a ceasefire that appears to have been disputed within hours of being announced.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: China’s growth stocks lose their shine as CICC tilts towards dividend payers
item.description:
For China’s equity markets, CICC’s call points to continued rotation from high-flying growth names on the ChiNext and STAR boards towards dividend-paying stocks, a group typically dominated by banks, utilities, energy and telecom companies. That could support relative strength in dividend indexes even if the broader market stays volatile. The trigger points are largely external: US inflation data and Fed signals this week bear on the overseas liquidity concerns CICC cites, while Middle East escalation and doubts over AI spending would weigh most on the technology half of the trade. A strong run of global chip earnings could revive appetite for growth names and narrow the case for defensive positioning.

---

Earlier:

  • PBOC is expected to set the USD/CNY reference rate at 6.6977 – Reuters estimate
  • Weeeknd: EU plans 350,000 annual cap on Chinese hybrids after Beijing agrees 16-point deal

---

After a tech-led first half, CICC wants investors in China to hold their growth stocks in one hand and something steadier in the other.

Summary:

  • CICC says A-share technology growth stocks rallied in the first half of 2026, driven by the AI supply chain and high-end manufacturing
  • Since July, negative narratives around the global AI chain, expectations of tighter overseas liquidity and Middle East risk have triggered a notable correction in previously strong growth sectors
  • With growth-stock volatility higher and risk appetite weaker, the firm says the case for dividend-paying assets deserves re-evaluation
  • It expects a “technology plus dividends” dumbbell allocation to gain emphasis as a way to balance earnings growth, shareholder cash returns and stability
  • CICC favours tech companies with clear industry trends, durable advantages and proven earnings, and dividend stocks with stable cash flow, sustainable payouts and reasonable valuations

China International Capital Corp expects investors in China’s mainland stock market to place greater emphasis on a “technology plus dividends” dumbbell strategy, after a sharp pullback in growth stocks since July exposed the risks of a portfolio tilted heavily towards tech.

A dumbbell, or barbell, strategy concentrates holdings at two ends of the risk spectrum rather than in the middle: in this case, higher-growth technology stocks on one side and stable, dividend-paying companies on the other. The aim is to capture upside from structural growth themes while relying on dividend payers to cushion portfolios when markets turn volatile. 

In a research note, CICC said A-share technology growth stocks benefited in the first half of 2026 from strong conditions across the AI supply chain and high-end manufacturing, sustaining a structural rally. Since July, however, three pressures have combined to drive a notable correction in those previously strong sectors: rising negative narratives around the global AI industry chain, expectations of tighter overseas liquidity and increased geopolitical risk in the Middle East.

The liquidity concern reflects the global rate backdrop. The US Federal Reserve raised interest rates in September and markets are still weighing whether further increases will follow, making this week’s US inflation data and remarks from Fed Chair Kevin Warsh relevant to Chinese equities as well.

With growth-stock volatility higher and risk appetite weaker, CICC said the relative appeal of dividend assets deserves a fresh look. It argued that in an environment where overall growth is limited but pockets of strong structural growth remain, and where risk sentiment swings sharply, combining technology with dividends offers a way to balance earnings growth potential, shareholder cash returns and portfolio stability.

On implementation, the firm recommends focusing on technology companies with clear industry trends, durable competitive advantages and a demonstrated ability to deliver profits. For the dividend side, it favours high-quality companies with stable earnings and cash flow, sustainable payout policies and reasonable valuations.

Whether the rotation deepens is likely to depend on the external triggers CICC identified, particularly the direction of US monetary policy and how the global AI earnings season unfolds over the coming weeks.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Deutsche Bank’s CEO warns wins for AfD and Left in 3 state votes risk deterring investors
item.description:
For the DAX, Sewing’s remarks are unlikely to move the index on their own, since state governments do not set federal economic policy and the index is dominated by global exporters whose earnings depend more on world demand than on domestic politics. The more direct exposure is in German residential property stocks, where the Left Party’s expropriation pledge in Berlin adds headline risk to listed landlords with large holdings in the capital. Over time, a perception of rising political risk could add to the discount investors already apply to German assets, making the pace of Merz’s reforms a more important driver for domestically focused DAX and MDAX names.

---

Germany’s top banker is warning that investors don’t read the fine print of federalism: a shock in one state looks like a shock to the whole country.

Summary:

  • Deutsche Bank Chief Executive Christian Sewing said the rise of parties on the political extremes poses a significant risk to Germany and should not be played down
  • The AfD came close to an absolute majority in Saxony-Anhalt and took first place in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania last month
  • The Left Party scored its biggest win in Berlin’s city election, pledging to expropriate the holdings of residential property companies
  • Sewing said foreign investors are unlikely to distinguish between a state government and Germany as a whole
  • He urged Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s government to continue reforms to revive the economy, calling it the only answer to extremes on both sides

The head of Germany’s largest bank has warned that recent state election victories for parties on the political extremes could drive away foreign investors, urging the federal government to keep pressing ahead with economic reforms.

Deutsche Bank Chief Executive Christian Sewing told the Bild daily (info via Reuters) that the rise of the far right and far left poses a significant risk to Germany that should not be downplayed. He argued that foreign investors cannot be expected to draw a clear line between a single state government and the country as a whole, and said that perception was understandable from an investor’s point of view.

The comments follow a series of state elections last month. The AfD, which wants to restrict immigration and return asylum seekers, and which security services classify as extremist in some regions, narrowly missed an absolute majority in the state parliament of Saxony-Anhalt. Two weeks later, it took first place in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania. In Berlin, the Left Party won its biggest victory in the city government election on a pledge to tackle soaring housing costs by expropriating the holdings of residential property companies.

Sewing said developments in both Saxony-Anhalt and Berlin were neither conducive to economic growth nor investment-friendly. Economists have also accused the AfD of fostering a climate that could deter the skilled workers and foreign capital the German economy needs.

The Berlin pledge revives a long-running debate in the capital. Berlin voters backed a non-binding 2021 referendum calling for large landlords’ flats to be taken into public ownership, though it was never implemented. The Left Party’s win puts the issue back on the agenda with a party in a stronger position to pursue it.

Sewing called on Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s government to continue its reform programme, describing it as the only response to extremists on both the right and left. The warning lands as Germany’s economy struggles to regain momentum, with investors watching whether Berlin can deliver reforms quickly enough to offset concerns about the political climate.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: MUFG: US CPI seen at 3.6%, core must surprise to revive an October Fed hike
item.description:
MUFG’s framing underlines that energy is almost the entire story behind rising US headline inflation since the Iran conflict began, keeping crude prices tightly linked to Fed expectations. The core reading is the trigger for rates markets: an in-line 0.2% would likely keep October hike pricing subdued and leave the dollar and Treasury yields range-bound, while a repeat of August’s 0.3% would revive bets on a back-to-back move and lift the front end. Strong retail sales on Thursday would reinforce the case that the economy can absorb tighter policy. Warsh’s comments early Friday could then reset expectations either way ahead of the October 27-28 meeting.

---

Earlier:

  • US CPI preview: energy set to lift inflation to 3.7%, core seen steady at 2.4%

---

Energy is doing the damage to the headline; the Fed’s real question this week is whether anything else is starting to burn.

Summary:

  • MUFG expects US headline inflation to rise to 3.6% in September, driven almost entirely by higher energy prices since the US-Iran conflict began
  • Core inflation is forecast to ease to 0.2% month on month after August’s services-driven 0.3% rise
  • MUFG says another upside surprise in core would likely be needed to revive expectations of a back-to-back Fed hike this month
  • Retail sales on Thursday are expected to confirm that consumer spending grew strongly in the third quarter
  • Fed Chair Warsh speaks at the IMF Annual Meetings in Bangkok early Friday, his first public remarks since the September FOMC meeting

Wednesday’s US inflation report is the main economic release of the week, and MUFG says the key question is not how high headline inflation climbs but whether price pressures are beginning to spread beyond energy.

The bank expects the September consumer price index to show headline inflation rising to 3.6%. It notes that the increase since the start of the US-Iran conflict has been driven almost entirely by higher energy prices, so the Federal Reserve and markets will focus on core inflation for any tentative signs of broadening. The report is due at 12:30 GMT (8:30 ET).

Core inflation, which strips out food and energy, picked up to 0.3% month on month in August, led by services. MUFG expects it to ease back to 0.2% in September. The bank says another upside surprise would likely be needed to revive market expectations of a back-to-back rate hike as soon as this month, following the Fed’s increase to a 3.75% to 4.00% target range in September.

Those expectations have already faded. Bets on an October move fell sharply after September payrolls showed only 29,000 jobs added, leaving a December hike as the market’s main scenario. A firm core reading would challenge that view; an in-line one would likely reinforce it.

Retail sales for September, due on Thursday at 12:30 GMT (8:30 ET), are expected to confirm that consumer spending continued to grow strongly in the third quarter, a sign the economy has so far absorbed higher energy costs and tighter policy.

The week ends with Fed Chair Kevin Warsh, who is scheduled to take part in a fireside chat at the IMF Annual Meetings in Bangkok at around 04:30 GMT on Friday (00:30 ET). He has not spoken publicly since the September meeting, so his remarks will be scrutinised for guidance ahead of the October 27-28 decision. Warsh has moved the Fed away from explicit forward guidance, so markets are likely to focus on his tone on inflation rather than any signal on timing. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: PBOC is expected to set the USD/CNY reference rate at 6.6977 – Reuters estimate
item.description:
The People’s Bank of China publishes its daily USD/CNY reference rate at around 0115 GMT (2115 US Eastern time the previous evening), and the number has become one of the most closely followed signals in Asian currency markets. Its importance has grown over the past month as Beijing has moved from holding back the yuan’s rise to steering it gradually higher.

---

Earlier:

  • Weeeknd: EU plans 350,000 annual cap on Chinese hybrids after Beijing agrees 16-point deal

---

Under China’s managed float, the onshore yuan may trade up to 2% either side of the midpoint set each morning. The central bank arrives at that midpoint by weighing the previous session’s close, moves in the US dollar and other major currencies, wider global FX conditions, and domestic priorities including capital flows, growth and financial stability. Because the calculation leaves room for judgement, the fixing doubles as a tool for shaping expectations.

Once the rate is published, onshore trading proceeds within the band. If pressure drives the yuan toward either limit, the PBOC can respond by buying or selling the currency directly, adjusting liquidity, or acting through state-owned banks. That is why markets treat the fixing as a statement of intent. A midpoint stronger than forecast usually signals resistance to depreciation, while a weaker one can point to acceptance of a softer yuan, or discomfort with how quickly it is gaining.

For close to a year, the second message prevailed. The PBOC consistently set the midpoint weaker than market forecasts, which traders took as an effort to slow appreciation. That gap was at its widest since February in late August, soon after the yuan hit a three-and-a-half-year high against the dollar.

September marked a turning point. The central bank lifted the fixing for eight sessions in a row, its longest run since 2023, taking the midpoint to its strongest since February 2023. The onshore yuan climbed to levels last seen in January 2023 and the offshore rate to its firmest since July 2022. Yet the fixing is still being set well below estimates, at one point by more than 500 pips against a Reuters survey, suggesting Beijing is easing the brakes rather than releasing them.

Goldman Sachs analysts tied the firmer fixings to the run-up to the recent Trump-Xi summit, a pattern they said matches past diplomacy, and expect policymakers to remain comfortable with steady, gradual gains.

The trade-off has not changed. A stronger yuan supports capital stability and lowers import costs, but rapid gains could hurt exporters while the domestic economy remains soft. The daily gap between the fixing and consensus forecasts remains the clearest guide to how far Beijing will let the yuan run, and whether that tolerance outlasts the summit

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: UBS: AI demand holds firm, with hyperscaler cloud growth tipped to hit 58%
item.description:
For equities, UBS’s view supports semiconductor and hardware names into an earnings season where results, rather than narrative, are expected to drive the AI trade. The near-term test arrives quickly, with ASML reporting on Wednesday and the major cloud providers later in the month, and any shortfall against the accelerating cloud growth UBS expects would likely hit richly valued megacaps hardest. Rates add a second risk: a hot US inflation print on Wednesday that lifts Treasury yields would weigh on long-duration tech valuations regardless of fundamentals. UBS’s preference for quality and defensive tech reflects that risk of sharp swings even within a supportive backdrop.

- UBS still sees the AI boom running on real demand, but after nearly five years it wants investors to be pickier about where they ride it.

Summary:

  • UBS says recent industry data continue to point to robust demand for AI compute and infrastructure
  • Meta’s Muse AI assistant has recorded more than 6.6 million downloads and 1.8 million daily active users in its first month, according to Sensor Tower data
  • TSMC reported a 51% rise in quarterly revenue, Samsung flagged an almost ninefold jump in operating profit, Hon Hai beat sales estimates and Marvell raised its fiscal 2028 revenue forecast
  • UBS expects average hyperscaler cloud revenue growth of 58% in the September quarter, up from 48% in the June quarter
  • The bank warns concerns over growth, financing and safety could cause bouts of volatility
  • It recommends a diversified approach favouring quality chip and hardware names, megacap platforms and defensive tech

Demand for artificial intelligence remains robust and fundamentals are likely to drive the AI trade through the coming earnings season, according to UBS, which pointed to strong chipmaker results and early signs of consumer appetite for AI agents.

The bank highlighted Meta’s Muse AI assistant, which has recorded more than 6.6 million downloads and 1.8 million daily active users since its launch a month ago, according to data from Sensor Tower. AI agents are tools that can carry out tasks on a user’s behalf rather than simply answering questions. UBS said it was too early to judge uptake of other recently launched agents, but described the early numbers as an encouraging sign that wider adoption could add further to AI demand.

Semiconductor results point the same way. TSMC reported a 51% rise in quarterly revenue, while Samsung flagged an almost ninefold jump in quarterly operating profit ahead of its full results. AI server assembler Hon Hai Precision Industry beat sales estimates, and chip designer Marvell raised its fiscal 2028 revenue forecast. UBS expects third-quarter earnings to provide further evidence of strong demand for AI compute and infrastructure.

Monetisation by the hyperscalers, the largest cloud computing providers, will be a key focus. UBS expects their average cloud revenue growth to accelerate to 58% year on year in the September quarter from 48% in the June quarter. It sees consumer AI agents as a potential next growth driver, opening revenue streams from subscriptions, advertising and transactions, and argues broader adoption would lift cloud utilisation, creating a clearer link between heavy infrastructure spending and revenue.

UBS acknowledged the risks. As the AI trade approaches its fifth year, it said concerns over growth, financing and safety could continue to trigger periods of volatility. It advised investors to stay engaged with what it sees as a structural opportunity while becoming more selective, favouring a diversified approach built around high-quality semiconductor and hardware beneficiaries of AI spending, megacap platforms and defensive technology companies.

The view will be tested quickly, with ASML reporting on Wednesday and the major cloud providers due later in the month.

---

Key terms explained

AI agents: Software that can carry out tasks on a user’s behalf, such as booking, buying or organising, rather than simply answering questions like a chatbot. Because they act as well as respond, they open up new ways for companies to earn money, from subscriptions to commissions on transactions.

Hyperscalers: The handful of giant technology companies that run the world’s largest cloud computing networks and rent out computing power and storage to businesses. They are the biggest buyers of AI chips and data centre equipment, so their spending and results are a key barometer for the whole AI trade.

AI compute: The raw processing power needed to train and run AI models, supplied mainly by specialised chips in large data centres. Rising demand for compute is what drives orders for chipmakers and server builders.

Monetisation: How companies turn AI investment into revenue. Investors have questioned whether the enormous sums spent on data centres will pay off, so evidence of AI-related sales growth is closely watched each earnings season.

Cloud utilisation: How much of a cloud provider’s installed capacity is actually being used and paid for. Higher utilisation means data centre spending is generating revenue rather than sitting idle.

AI server assembler: A manufacturer that builds the complete computer systems housing AI chips, combining processors, memory, cooling and networking into racks for data centres. Hon Hai, also known as Foxconn, is the largest.

Megacap platforms: The very largest listed technology companies, each worth well over a trillion dollars, whose products reach billions of users and give them scale to profit from AI.

Defensive tech: Technology companies with steadier, less cyclical earnings, such as established software or services firms, that tend to hold up better when markets turn volatile.

---

What is hyperscaler cloud growth?

The companies: Hyperscalers are the handful of technology giants that run the world’s largest cloud computing networks, chiefly Amazon Web Services, Microsoft Azure and Google Cloud. They rent computing power, storage and AI tools to businesses over the internet, so customers don’t need to build their own data centres.

What the growth figure measures: Hyperscaler cloud growth is the year-on-year increase in revenue from these cloud businesses. Analysts often average it across the main providers to gauge how fast demand for cloud services, and increasingly AI services, is expanding.

Why it matters for AI: The hyperscalers are spending tens of billions of dollars a year on data centres and AI chips. Their cloud revenue growth is the clearest sign of whether that spending is paying off. Faster growth suggests customers are actually using and paying for AI capacity; slowing growth would raise questions about overbuilding.

Why markets watch it: Because the hyperscalers are the biggest buyers of AI chips and servers, their cloud results ripple through the entire AI supply chain, from chipmakers such as TSMC to server builders such as Hon Hai.

Where it stands: UBS expects average hyperscaler cloud revenue growth to accelerate to 58% year on year in the September quarter, up from 48% in the June quarter. The figures will be tested when the major cloud providers report later this month.

"The most advanced AI on the planet and the desk head tells me to go fetch his dry cleaning."

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Weeeknd: EU plans 350,000 annual cap on Chinese hybrids after Beijing agrees 16-point deal
item.description:
For European carmakers, a hybrid quota offers some relief from lower-priced Chinese competition at a time when Volkswagen, Stellantis, Mercedes and BMW are under pressure on profits, though the cap’s generous starting size and annual increases limit how much market share it protects. Chinese brands that have leaned on hybrids to sidestep EU electric vehicle tariffs face slower European growth, with Chery among the most exposed. The bigger risk for markets is Thursday’s summit: a push by Germany and France for broader trade tools could invite retaliation, and Beijing’s control of rare earth supplies gives it leverage over the same European manufacturers the quota is meant to protect.

---

Beijing has given Brussels a hybrid car quota and kept almost everything else, buying time before EU leaders decide how hard to push.

Summary:

  • The EU plans to limit imports of Chinese hybrid vehicles to 350,000 a year, with the quota rising 6% annually from the second year and lasting four years
  • The aim is for the safeguards to apply from December 1; they would technically cover hybrids from all countries to comply with WTO rules, with China’s quota at least as large as any other exporter’s
  • The move follows a 16-point China-EU consensus on trade and investment reached in Beijing on Friday, with further talks planned for January and March
  • Chinese brands took about a quarter of European hybrid sales in August, partly because hybrids escaped the EU’s 2024 tariffs on electric vehicles
  • Analysts see the deal as a win for Beijing, which conceded little on the drivers of an EU trade deficit of more than €1 billion a day
  • EU leaders meet in Brussels on Thursday to consider a tougher response, with Germany and France pushing for stronger trade defence tools

The European Union plans to cap imports of Chinese hybrid cars at 350,000 a year, after Beijing agreed to curb exports as part of a 16-point trade and investment consensus reached in talks that ended on Friday.

The proposed safeguards could take effect from December 1, Bloomberg News reported, citing a document outlining the measures. The quota would rise by 6% a year from the second year and remain in place for four years. To comply with World Trade Organization rules against discrimination, the limits would technically apply to hybrid imports from all countries, with China receiving a quota at least as large as any other exporter. Safeguards of this kind usually take the form of tariff-rate quotas, which leave imports below a set volume untouched and apply a levy to anything above it.

The agreement followed talks in Beijing between EU trade chief Maros Sefcovic and Chinese Commerce Minister Wang Wentao. Chinese hybrid shipments have surged partly because they escaped the tariffs Brussels imposed on fully electric vehicles in 2024, and Chinese brands accounted for about a quarter of European hybrid sales in August. EU ambassadors briefed on Sunday broadly welcomed the outcome but described it as only the start of efforts to rebalance trade.

Analysts were less impressed. One China-focused research firm called the deal a strategic win for Beijing, arguing that beyond vehicles and modest tariff relief it does little to change China’s trading terms with Europe, while buying time for further talks in January and March. A trade law specialist said the timing suggested China wanted to ease tensions before EU leaders meet, and warned that WTO-compliant remedies often have limited impact on overall trade flows.

The stakes for European industry are high. The EU’s trade deficit with China now exceeds €1 billion a day, and European carmakers are among the weakest performers globally. Mercedes-Benz car sales fell 8% in the third quarter, and Volkswagen cut its profit forecast last month. Renault Chief Executive Francois Provost welcomed the deal as a milestone, saying that without it Europe would face a damaging trade war.

EU leaders meet in Brussels on Thursday to decide whether to go further, after Germany and France called for stronger tools, including one that could restrict China’s access to the single market. Beijing has warned against protectionism, and its dominance of rare earth supplies gives it a powerful lever should Europe escalate.

---

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: US CPI preview: energy set to lift inflation to 3.7%, core seen steady at 2.4%
item.description:
Wednesday’s report is a direct read on how far the Iran war’s energy shock is feeding into US consumer prices, and a hot energy component would reinforce the link between crude risk and Fed policy. Treasury markets are likely to trade the core number rather than the headline: a soft core would favour the front end and weigh on the dollar, while a firm one would revive October hike pricing that faded after weak payrolls. Gold would likely benefit from a soft core and lower yields. With Brent still above $100 and fresh attacks on Saudi infrastructure, energy-driven inflation risk extends well beyond this release.

--

September’s CPI is set to look alarming on the surface and calm underneath, and the Fed has to decide which one to believe.

Summary:

  • US September CPI is due Wednesday at 12:30 GMT (8:30 ET), the last inflation report before the Fed’s October 27-28 meeting
  • The market expects headline CPI to rise 0.6% on the month, lifting the annual rate to around 3.7% from 3.4%
  • Core inflation is forecast to slow to around 0.2% on the month, holding at 2.4% annually
  • Energy is expected to jump around 5.5%, led by gasoline, while food stays subdued
  • Odds of an October Fed hike have fallen to around one in four after weak September payrolls, with December still largely priced
  • Fed Chair Warsh speaks in Bangkok early Friday, his final scheduled remarks before the meeting

US consumer prices are expected to post their sharpest monthly rise since April when September inflation data is released on Wednesday, driven almost entirely by energy, while underlying inflation is forecast to stay subdued.

The market expects headline CPI to climb 0.6% in September, according to Westpac’s calendar, up from 0.4% in August. That would lift the annual rate to around 3.7% from 3.4%, a four-month high. The Cleveland Fed’s inflation nowcast points in the same direction, at about 0.5% for the month and 3.6% on the year. The report is due at 12:30 GMT (8:30 ET).

Energy is the main driver. Analysts expect energy prices to rise around 5.5% in the month, led by gasoline, which would be the largest energy contribution since March. In August, gasoline prices were already up more than 27% on a year earlier.

Core inflation, which excludes food and energy, is expected to tell a calmer story. Forecasts point to a rise of around 0.2%, slower than August’s 0.3%, keeping the annual core rate at 2.4%. August’s core reading was boosted by a one-off jump in telephone services following a methodology change, and analysts expect volatile items such as hotel prices and used cars to correct. Airfares are the exception, rising as higher jet fuel costs pass through to ticket prices.

That split puts the Federal Reserve in an awkward position. The Fed raised its target range to 3.75%-4.00% on September 16, but the odds of a follow-up move at the October 27-28 meeting fell to around one in four after September payrolls showed only 29,000 jobs added. Markets still largely price a December hike. Goldman Sachs had expected one more increase in October, though that view assumed oil would fall towards $85, and Brent remains above $100.

A firm core reading alongside the energy-driven headline would likely revive October hike bets, while a soft core would reinforce expectations of a December move. Thursday’s producer prices and retail sales will add to the picture before Fed Chair Kevin Warsh speaks at the IMF meetings in Bangkok early Friday, his last scheduled appearance before the meeting.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: IEA urges faster diesel releases as 400m-barrel March pledge lags, board meets Oct 15
item.description:
For oil, the IEA’s focus confirms that the acute shortage sits in refined products rather than crude, which points to continued support for diesel margins even as Gulf crude flows recover. The European view that the G7 deal mostly repackages March pledges matters for pricing, since it implies fewer genuinely new barrels than the 100 million headline suggests and limits any relief to tightness. Tenders and the board’s decision this week will set expectations: concrete, front-loaded diesel volumes could cap distillate cracks, while vague commitments risk leaving prices elevated. Fresh disruption to Saudi supply would add pressure to an already strained product market.

--- Seven months after its biggest-ever stock release, the IEA is still chasing barrels, and this time it wants diesel first.

Summary:

  • IEA chief Fatih Birol urged members that have not fully delivered stocks pledged under the March collective action to accelerate releases, prioritising diesel
  • He asked all members, including those that have completed their pledges, to assess whether further diesel releases are needed and to set out scale and timing
  • Birol cited renewed attacks on civilian and energy infrastructure in Saudi Arabia, ahead of the agency’s October 15 governing board meeting
  • The G7 agreed this month to release up to 100 million barrels of diesel and crude after the Trump administration threatened Europe with a diesel export ban
  • EU countries broadly see the G7 deal as enacting March commitments rather than adding new volumes
  • In March, the IEA’s 32 members agreed to release 400 million barrels, the largest emergency release on record

The International Energy Agency has urged its members to speed up delivery of emergency oil stocks pledged in March and to consider releasing more diesel, as record fuel prices and fresh attacks on Saudi energy infrastructure tighten global markets.

In a statement ahead of the agency’s October 15 governing board meeting, Executive Director Fatih Birol called on governments that have yet to fully deliver their share of the March collective action to accelerate those releases where possible, with diesel given priority. He also asked all members, including those that have already met their pledges, to assess whether further diesel releases are needed and to set out how large they would be and when they would take place. Birol said current conditions merit immediate attention and are best handled through cooperation among members, pointing to renewed attacks on civilian and energy targets in Saudi Arabia.

The IEA’s 32 members agreed in March to release 400 million barrels from emergency reserves in response to the Iran war, the largest such action in the agency’s history. That some pledged volumes remain undelivered seven months later underlines how drawn out the effort has been.

Pressure has built since. After the Trump administration threatened European countries with a diesel export ban unless they did more to curb record prices, the Group of Seven agreed earlier this month to release as much as 100 million barrels of diesel and crude. European Union members, however, broadly view that deal as putting the March commitments into effect rather than adding new volumes.

The focus on diesel reflects where the strain is greatest. Gulf crude exports have largely recovered, but Goldman Sachs estimates that shipments of diesel, gasoline and jet fuel from the region remain around half of normal. Russia partially lifted its own diesel export ban over the weekend, clearing 500,000 tons for international buyers after an agreement between Presidents Putin and Trump.

The governing board meeting is the next test of whether IEA members can turn pledges into barrels quickly enough to ease record diesel prices, and whether any genuinely new volumes emerge beyond the March commitments.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Preview: RBA minutes and jobs data headline Australia’s week ahead, with unemployment seen at 4.6%
item.description:
For the Australian dollar and front-end rates, the minutes carry more weight than usual because Bullock’s post-meeting tone was softer than the decision itself. A record that leans toward holding would support pricing for a pause and could weigh on the currency, while one that keeps further tightening clearly on the table would reinforce Westpac’s call for another move by year-end. Oil is the swing factor behind both outcomes, as the board explicitly cited Middle East pressure on fuel prices, so any renewed crude strength from Gulf attacks would harden the inflation case. An upside surprise in unemployment would sharpen the market’s focus on downside risks to growth.

---

Four hikes in, the question for Australia this week is whether the RBA’s resolve or its Governor’s softer words better describe where policy goes next.

Summary:

  • Minutes of the RBA’s September meeting, when the cash rate rose 25 basis points to 4.60%, are due Tuesday
  • CBA will be checking whether the minutes match the more dovish tone Governor Bullock struck afterwards, and says the hurdle for another hike is now higher
  • Westpac still expects one more increase, taking the cash rate to 4.85% by December
  • September labour force data on Thursday is expected to show unemployment steady at 4.6%, the highest since late 2021
  • Westpac forecasts 20,000 new jobs, matching consensus, while CBA expects a softer 10,000 after August’s surprise 40,000 gain
  • Consumer sentiment slumped after the September hike, and business conditions turned negative in August

Australia’s week centres on two releases that will shape expectations for the Reserve Bank’s next move: minutes of the September policy meeting on Tuesday and the September labour force survey on Thursday. Both are due at 11:30 am Sydney time, 00:30 GMT (8:30 pm ET the previous evening).

The RBA’s Monetary Policy Board lifted the cash rate by 25 basis points to 4.60% in September, a unanimous and widely expected decision that marked the fourth hike of the cycle. The board said inflation remained too high, pointing to domestic capacity pressures alongside global shocks from the Middle East conflict and the AI investment boom. It acknowledged that the economy was slowing and the labour market loosening, but not quickly enough to return inflation to target in a reasonable timeframe, especially with renewed pressure on oil prices.

CBA says the minutes should shed light on the arguments for holding rates steady, and it will be watching whether they match the more dovish tone Governor Michele Bullock struck at her press conference, when she noted that the four hikes would take time to flow through. CBA views the hurdle for another increase as now higher. Westpac takes a firmer line, forecasting one more hike to 4.85% by December, and says markets will look to the minutes for guidance on the outlook.

The hike has already hit households. Westpac’s consumer sentiment index fell 4.7% to 80.4 in October, near the weakest levels in the survey’s history, with confidence among those surveyed after the decision far below those polled before it.

Thursday’s jobs data follows a surprise jump of around 40,000 in August that nevertheless pushed unemployment up to 4.6%, the highest since late 2021, as participation rose to 67.1%, just below its record. Westpac forecasts a 20,000 rise in September, in line with consensus, with participation easing to 67.0% and unemployment steady at 4.6%. It says cost-of-living pressures and higher rates are drawing more people into the workforce, keeping labour supply ahead of demand.

CBA expects a smaller 10,000 gain, noting its own internal data had jobs growth closer to 20,000 a month, and also sees unemployment at 4.6%. It warns the print could be noisier than usual: a survey group with a very low jobless rate is rotating out, an upside risk, while August’s rise may have been overstated and could partly reverse. CBA cautions against reading any fall in unemployment as a change in trend, expecting the rate to drift higher as the economy slows.

Elsewhere, the NAB business survey on Tuesday follows August’s slide in conditions into negative territory for the first time in six years.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Goldman: Gulf oil exports back at 22-23 mb/d, but Dated Brent stays very high
item.description:
For oil, the split between recovering volumes and stubbornly high physical prices is the key tension. Restored crude flows argue for lower benchmark prices over time, but the premium in Dated Brent shows buyers are still paying up for prompt barrels to rebuild depleted inventories, which keeps the front of the curve steeply backwardated. Refined products remain the tightest corner, supporting diesel and jet margins even as crude supply normalises. The weekend’s Houthi claims against Saudi Aramco facilities are an immediate test, since Saudi barrels have led the recovery, and any confirmed disruption would likely widen the physical premium again.

---

The barrels are back, but the fear isn’t: Gulf exports have normalised while physical buyers keep paying war prices.

Summary:

  • Goldman Sachs estimates Persian Gulf oil exports, including dark exports, recovered to 22-23 mb/d over the past two weeks, broadly in line with their 2025 average
  • Physical Dated Brent prices remain very high despite the recovery
  • Crude has driven the rebound, with Saudi Arabia leading and Iran showing no seaborne crude exports in September
  • JPMorgan’s estimate is more conservative, at around 89% of 2025 levels, mainly due to how dark flows are counted
  • Exports of diesel, gasoline and jet fuel remain at roughly half of normal levels
  • Goldman still expects Brent to ease to $85 by year-end and $80 in 2027

Oil exports from the Persian Gulf have returned to roughly normal levels, but physical crude prices have yet to follow, according to Goldman Sachs. The bank estimates that Gulf exports, including so-called dark exports, have recovered to 22 to 23 million barrels per day over the past two weeks, broadly in line with their 2025 average, while physical Dated Brent remains very high.

Dark exports are cargoes carried by tankers that switch off their satellite transponders, making them hard to track. Goldman estimated these flows at around 5 million barrels per day in September, a large part of why its count is higher than others. JPMorgan, using a more conservative approach, put recent Gulf exports at about 89% of 2025 levels, with most of the difference coming down to how much of the dark fleet is included.

The recovery has been led by crude rather than refined products. In late September, Goldman said crude exports had climbed above their 2025 average, with Saudi shipments more than doubling during the month to nearly 12 million barrels per day and the UAE also exporting above normal. Satellite data showed no seaborne crude exports from Iran. Products are lagging badly: exports of diesel, gasoline and jet fuel remain around half of normal, which Goldman attributes to elevated regional refinery outages and the greater risk faced by smaller product tankers carrying more flammable cargo.

Physical prices tell a different story to the flow data. Dated Brent, the price for North Sea cargoes loading on specific dates, was recently near $120 a barrel, well above futures. Goldman links the gap to fears that escalation could damage long-term production and to record-low global stocks outside OECD commercial inventories, which have prompted buyers to rebuild supplies quickly. The bank estimates the risk premium in Brent spreads averaged $22 a barrel in September, the second-highest monthly level on record and above the peak during the 2022 Russia-Ukraine war.

Goldman maintains its base case that Brent eases to $85 by year-end and $80 in 2027, while warning that renewed escalation could push prices sharply higher. The weekend’s Houthi claims of strikes on Saudi Aramco facilities put that risk directly against the barrels that have driven the recovery.

Dated Brent is the spot price for physical North Sea cargoes loading on specific dates, as opposed to the front-month futures contract; in early April the spot premium over futures exceeded $25 a barrel. Normally that spread is narrow.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Weekend: Musk says $15 billion Terrafab can make chips better than anyone, given time
item.description:
For chip stocks, the remarks reinforce that Terrafab is a long-dated threat to incumbent foundries rather than a near-term one, which limits any read-across to TSMC and Samsung while Musk’s companies keep buying their output. Intel stands to gain the most direct benefit as a joint venture partner, giving its foundry ambitions a high-profile anchor customer. For Tesla, the project adds a large, open-ended capital commitment with a multi-year payoff, a factor investors will weigh against the strategic value of securing AI chip supply. Musk’s admission on timing may help temper expectations that had run ahead of execution.

---

Earlier:

  • Why a few words from Elon Musk can (and did!) move a $600 billion+ chipmaker
  • SpaceX just officially announced two massive milestones for Starlink Mobile

---

Musk still thinks he can beat the world’s chipmakers at their own game, but for once he isn’t promising to do it quickly.

Summary:

  • Musk said his companies would probably work out how to make chips better than anyone, citing their expertise in custom equipment, but conceded it could take quite a few years
  • Terrafab is planned for Grimes, Texas, as a joint venture between Tesla and SpaceX alongside Intel, with an initial investment of more than $15 billion
  • The 100 million square foot facility will be built in phases on around 3,000 acres; SpaceX controls more than 13,000 acres at the site
  • State filings point to a construction start on December 1, 2026, and completion by the end of 2028
  • SpaceX shares recently climbed back above their $135 IPO price, making Musk the world’s first trillionaire

Elon Musk said his companies would probably work out how to make semiconductors better than anyone, citing their experience building customised manufacturing equipment, but conceded that reaching that point could take quite a few years, Bloomberg (gated) reported on Saturday.

Speaking at an X event over the weekend, Musk described chipmaking as one of the hardest things to do in the world and said he did not want to sound complacent. The measured tone contrasts with the project’s launch in Austin in March, when he billed Terrafab as the most ambitious chip-building effort in history and argued that global fabrication capacity covered only around 2% of what Tesla and SpaceX would need.

Terrafab is set to be built in Grimes County, Texas, roughly an hour northwest of Houston, as a joint venture between Tesla and SpaceX alongside Intel. Bloomberg put the initial investment at more than $15 billion. The facility is planned at 100 million square feet and will be built in phases on a footprint of about 3,000 acres, although SpaceX controls more than 13,000 acres at the site. Texas government filings in September listed a planned construction start of December 1, 2026, with completion targeted for the end of 2028.

Cost estimates have varied widely. Texas Governor Greg Abbott said in August that the first phase would involve nearly $17 billion in capital investment and create 3,000 jobs, while earlier county filings referred to far larger sums across all phases.

The plant’s main purpose is high-volume production of Tesla’s AI5 chips, reducing reliance on outside foundries such as TSMC and Samsung that Musk’s companies currently compete with every other technology group to access. Musk has said they will keep buying from existing suppliers in the meantime.

The comments came as SpaceX, which listed in June, moved back above its $135 initial public offering price, a gain that made Musk the world’s first trillionaire. With construction yet to begin, the December start date will be the first concrete test of whether Terrafab keeps to its stated schedule. 

What is Terrafab?

The project: Terrafab is a planned semiconductor manufacturing complex backed by Elon Musk’s companies, run as a joint venture between Tesla and SpaceX with Intel as a partner. Tesla’s own materials spell it “Terafab.”

Why Musk wants it: Musk argues existing chipmakers cannot expand fast enough to supply the AI chips his companies need for self-driving cars, Optimus humanoid robots, AI data centres and planned solar-powered satellites. He has said current global capacity covers only a small fraction of that demand.

What makes it different: The plan is to bring the whole process under one roof, from chip design and fabrication of logic and memory chips through to packaging and testing. Most of the industry splits these steps across separate companies and sites. Musk says this would let his teams design, test and revise chips far faster.

What it will make: Two broad types of chip: one for robots and vehicles, and a radiation-hardened version designed for computing in orbit. The first priority is volume production of Tesla’s AI5 chip.

Where and when: The main site is in Grimes County, Texas, northwest of Houston, preceded by a smaller research fab at Tesla’s Austin plant, where ground was broken in April. State filings point to construction starting in December 2026 and finishing by the end of 2028.

The big caveat: Musk’s companies have no track record in chip manufacturing, one of the most complex and capital-intensive industries in the world, and Musk himself now says mastering it could take years.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: More on Russia’s diesel U-turn: 500,000 tons cleared for export after Trump-Putin deal
item.description:
For oil product, the immediate volume is modest: around 500,000 tons equals roughly 3.7 million barrels, small against global diesel trade, so the price effect rests more on what follows than on this tranche. The signal matters more for middle distillate margins, as a Russian return to export markets, alongside a pause in Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries, would ease one of the tighter corners of the fuel market. Buyers may move cautiously, since US sanctions passed last month still target Russian energy revenues and contract terms remain unclear. Any confirmation of further tranches would add downside pressure to diesel cracks in Europe and Asia.

--- Moscow has turned on the diesel tap, but only partway, and on its own schedule rather than the one Trump announced.

Summary:

  • Russia partially lifted its diesel export ban with immediate effect on Saturday, allowing 500,000 metric tons to reach international markets
  • The move follows Friday’s agreement between Putin and Trump for Russia to supply the US and global markets
  • Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak said production is sufficient to cover domestic demand in full as well as the agreed exports
  • Russian oil companies will begin negotiating export contracts immediately, in coordination with the government
  • The government gave no shipping timeline and did not say whether further volumes would be approved
  • Russia banned diesel exports by non-producers on January 31 and extended the ban to producers on July 9 to protect domestic supply

Russia has partially lifted its ban on diesel exports with immediate effect, clearing 500,000 metric tons of fuel for international markets after President Vladimir Putin and US President Donald Trump agreed on Friday that Russia would supply the US and global buyers, according to a Russian government statement on Saturday.

Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak said Russian output was sufficient to meet domestic demand in full while also supporting exports at the agreed volumes. Russian oil companies will begin negotiating export contracts with foreign buyers straight away, working in coordination with the government.

The decision partly reverses restrictions Moscow imposed this year to protect its domestic fuel market. Russia first barred diesel exports by non-producers on January 31 and widened the ban to producers on July 9. Novak’s assurance on domestic supply is notable given that those restrictions were introduced precisely because home supply was under strain.

The volume released is smaller and less defined than the schedule Trump set out on Friday. He said Russia would supply more than 300,000 tons immediately, 500,000 tons in November, 1 million tons after that and a further 3 million tons later, a total of about 4.8 million tons. The Russian statement covers only 500,000 tons, gives no shipping dates and does not say whether further volumes will be authorised. At a standard conversion, 500,000 tons is roughly 3.7 million barrels.

The move comes alongside Trump’s announcement on Sunday of an energy ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine, which Kyiv said it supports. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky had earlier offered to halt attacks on Russian diesel facilities if Moscow stopped its own strikes, a trade that, if it holds, could also ease pressure on Russian refining capacity.

The reversal sits awkwardly with the sweeping sanctions law Trump signed last month targeting Russian oil and gas revenues. Whether further export tranches follow, and how buyers weigh sanctions risk when negotiating contracts, will determine how much Russian diesel actually reaches global markets in the weeks ahead.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Monday: Thin start for Asia as Tokyo shuts for Sports Day and US Treasuries stay closed. A huge week follows.
item.description:
Monday’s closures in Tokyo and the US cash Treasury market mean thinner liquidity across Asia and into the US session, which can exaggerate moves on weekend headlines from Saudi Arabia, Russia and Ukraine.

  • Singapore, Hong Kong, Australia and New Zealand are all open though

For oil, the week links directly to inflation: energy has been the main force holding US headline CPI above 3%, so any renewed crude strength from Gulf attacks would feed expectations of further Fed tightening, while the Russian diesel deal and energy ceasefire point the other way for fuel prices. A hot CPI print would likely lift the front end of the Treasury curve and support the dollar, putting pressure on the yen. Bank results offer an early read on credit quality under higher rates.

---

A quiet Monday in Tokyo and on the Treasury desk gives way to the week’s real business: inflation, the banks and one last hearing from Warsh.

Summary:

  • Japan is closed Monday for Sports Day; in the US, Columbus Day shuts the cash Treasury market while equities trade normally
  • US September CPI is due Wednesday at 12:30 GMT (8:30 ET), the last inflation reading before the October 27-28 FOMC meeting
  • August CPI rose 0.4% on the month and 3.4% on the year, driven by gasoline, while core held at 0.3% monthly and 2.4% annually
  • JPMorgan, Goldman Sachs, Wells Fargo and Citi report Tuesday, with Bank of America, Morgan Stanley and BlackRock on Wednesday
  • September PPI and retail sales follow on Thursday
  • Fed Chair Warsh speaks at the IMF meetings in Bangkok early Friday, his final scheduled appearance before the pre-meeting blackout

Markets open the week with holidays on both sides of the Pacific. Japan is closed on Monday for Sports Day, leaving Tokyo’s equity and bond markets shut, while the US observes Columbus Day, when equity markets stay open but the federal debt market is closed. The closures leave Asian liquidity thin at the start of a week that builds steadily toward a US inflation report and a final pre-meeting appearance from Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh.

The calendar shifts quickly to the US on Tuesday, when JPMorgan Chase, Goldman Sachs, Wells Fargo, Citigroup, UnitedHealth Group and Johnson & Johnson all report before the open, offering an early view on credit conditions and lending demand after the Fed’s September rate rise. Bank of America, Morgan Stanley and BlackRock follow on Wednesday, alongside ASML.

Wednesday’s September CPI release at 12:30 GMT (8:30 ET) is the week’s centrepiece, as it is the latest inflation reading before the FOMC meeting on October 28. The August report set a firm baseline: headline prices rose 0.4% on the month after 0.1% in July, with gasoline accounting for more than a third of the increase, while core prices rose 0.3%. On an annual basis, headline inflation held at 3.4% and core eased to 2.4%, with energy up about 16% over the year. Forecasts for September point to energy pushing the headline higher again, with one forecaster expecting a 0.6% monthly rise that would lift the annual rate to roughly 3.7%. A broad consensus had not yet been published.

Thursday brings September producer prices and advance retail sales, both at 8:30 ET (12:30 GMT).

Warsh then gets the final word. He is due to take part in a moderated conversation at the IMF and World Bank Annual Meetings in Bangkok around 04:30 GMT on Friday (00:30 ET), described as a public appearance before the blackout period ahead of the October 27-28 FOMC meeting. Since taking office, Warsh has sought to change how the Fed communicates, moving away from forward guidance while stressing its commitment to price stability, so markets will look to his tone rather than any signal on timing.

The combination matters because energy, not core inflation, is doing most of the work in the headline. A hot print driven by fuel costs would leave Warsh weighing an energy shock against still-moderate underlying inflation, two weeks before the meeting and shortly before the US midterm elections.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Trump says Russia, Ukraine agree energy ceasefire two days after Russian diesel deal
item.description:
For oil, the two announcements point the same way for diesel: more Russian supply. The deal adds Russian barrels directly, while a halt to Ukrainian strikes on Russian fuel infrastructure would remove a recurring threat to the country’s refining and export capacity, a combination that would weigh on diesel margins if it holds. Traders are likely to discount both until details emerge, as the Kremlin has not publicly confirmed the truce terms and the delivery schedule rests on Trump’s own description. The broader signal is a weaker US commitment to squeezing Russian energy revenues, which erodes part of the sanctions-related risk premium in crude.

---

Earlier:

  • Houthi strike on Riyadh airport kills 13, group claims Aramco hits. Saudi, Iran talking now.
  • Delivered crude prices surge back to highs as JPMorgan flags tanker crunch

---

In the space of a weekend, Washington went from sanctioning Russian energy to buying it, then declared a truce over it.

Summary:

  • Trump announced on Sunday that Russia and Ukraine had agreed an immediate energy ceasefire; Ukrainian officials said they learned of it from his social media post
  • Zelensky said Ukraine supports the ceasefire and is waiting for details from the US, after earlier offering to stop striking Russian diesel facilities if Russia stopped its attacks
  • On Friday, Trump said he had struck a deal with Putin for Russia to supply diesel in stages: more than 300,000 tons immediately, 500,000 tons in November, 1 million tons after that and a further 3 million tons later
  • The deal reverses a sweeping Russia sanctions law Trump signed last month targeting Moscow’s oil and gas revenues, and comes as high US fuel prices loom over the midterm elections
  • Zelensky called the diesel deal a weak decision by strong partners, saying it would prolong the war
  • The announcements coincided with Miami talks between Ukrainian officials and US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner on a plan to end the war

President Donald Trump said on Sunday that Russia and Ukraine had agreed to an immediate “energy ceasefire,” an announcement that appeared to catch Kyiv by surprise and came just two days after he unveiled a deal for Russia to supply the United States with diesel.

Trump posted the truce on social media, saying both sides had agreed and warning them not to break it. A Ukrainian official told CNN that Kyiv had learned of it the same way the public had, by reading the post. The White House and Kremlin had not explained how the agreement was reached or what it covers.

Zelensky said Ukraine supported the ceasefire, that Russia needed to do the same, and that Kyiv was awaiting details from Washington. He said he had discussed the news with Canada’s Mark Carney, Finland’s Alexander Stubb and NATO chief Mark Rutte. Earlier on Sunday he had told ABC News that Ukraine would stop attacking Russian diesel facilities if Russia halted its attacks, describing that as a fair trade.

The truce follows a more contentious announcement on Friday. After a phone call with Russian President Vladimir Putin, Trump said Russia would supply more than 300,000 tons of diesel immediately, 500,000 tons in November, 1 million tons after that and a further 3 million tons soon afterwards. That totals about 4.8 million tons, or roughly 36 million barrels at a standard conversion rate.

The deal marks a sharp turn from the sweeping sanctions law Trump signed last month aimed at choking off the oil and gas revenues that fund Russia’s war. It is also aimed at high domestic fuel prices ahead of next month’s midterm elections. Zelensky described it as a weak decision by strong partners and said it would prolong the war. Both announcements landed while US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner were holding talks with Ukrainian officials in Miami on a proposal to end the conflict.

Much now depends on details that have yet to surface: whether Moscow publicly commits to the truce, how it would be monitored, and whether the diesel shipments arrive on the schedule Trump set out. Without those, markets and Kyiv alike are working from a social media post.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Houthi strike on Riyadh airport kills 13, group claims Aramco hits. Saudi, Iran talking now.
item.description:
For oil, the shift in targeting matters more than the airport damage: claimed strikes on two Aramco facilities and a confirmed hit on Dammam bring the conflict into the Eastern Province, the centre of Saudi crude output. With Aramco silent, traders are left to price the risk without knowing whether any production or export capacity was affected, which tends to support a geopolitical premium until damage is clarified. The timing adds pressure, as JPMorgan noted last week that the global tanker fleet is already close to full use, so any disruption to Gulf loadings or routing would land on a market with little shipping slack. The Saudi-Iranian contact is the main counterweight, and any sign of de-escalation could quickly erode that premium.

---

The Houthis are no longer just hitting Riyadh’s runways; they say they are now aiming at the kingdom’s oil, and Riyadh has picked up the phone to Tehran.

Summary:

  • Yemen’s Iran-aligned Houthis claimed a Saturday strike on Riyadh’s international airport that killed 13 people and wounded more than 300, the third attack on the airport in a week
  • A projectile hit Terminal 4 on Sunday, causing a fire and injuries, while Saudi defences intercepted a cruise missile near the airport and a drone in the Eastern Province
  • The Houthis said they also struck Dammam’s King Fahd International Airport and two Saudi Aramco facilities; Saudi authorities confirmed the Dammam strike, while Aramco did not comment
  • Trump said the US was considering joining Saudi strikes on the Houthis, and the group warned of a stronger response to further Saudi action
  • Riyadh airport remains closed and schools have moved online until Thursday, though an international energy conference went ahead
  • Saudi Arabia’s foreign minister discussed de-escalation with his Iranian counterpart, their first publicly reported contact since the Houthi strikes intensified

Saudi Arabia’s foreign minister has spoken with his Iranian counterpart about the regional escalation and efforts to ease tensions, Saudi state media reported on Sunday, in their first publicly reported contact since Yemen’s Iran-aligned Houthis stepped up attacks on the kingdom. The call came after a weekend in which the Houthis claimed a deadly strike on Riyadh’s main airport and said they had widened their targets to include Saudi oil facilities.

The Houthis claimed responsibility for Saturday’s attack on Riyadh’s international airport, which killed 13 people and wounded more than 300, according to Saudi authorities and India’s embassy, which said one of its injured citizens had died. It was the third attack on the airport in a week, after two earlier strikes killed four people. On Sunday, an unidentified projectile hit Terminal 4 and caused a fire, injuring an unspecified number of people, while Saudi air defences intercepted a cruise missile near the airport and a drone in the Eastern Province.

Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Saree said the group had also struck the airport in Dammam and two Saudi Aramco facilities. Saudi aviation authorities confirmed a strike on Dammam’s King Fahd International Airport, which a witness told Reuters hit the tarmac beside parked aircraft at around 1730 GMT (1:30 p.m. ET). Aramco and the Saudi government’s media office did not respond to requests for comment, so the claimed strikes on oil facilities remain unverified.

That claim is the most significant development for energy markets. Dammam serves the capital of the Eastern Province, the heart of Saudi oil production, and the region has been hit before: the 2019 drone and missile attack on the Abqaiq processing plant briefly knocked out roughly half of Saudi output, showing how concentrated the kingdom’s infrastructure is.

The escalation follows a stepped-up Saudi campaign in Yemen after the Houthis seized strategic territory along the Red Sea coast last month. The group said Saudi Arabia carried out 124 air strikes in a single day and warned that worse would follow unless the strikes stopped. US President Donald Trump said Washington was considering joining the Saudi campaign, a spillover from the wider war with Iran that the US and Israel began in February.

Daily life in Riyadh is adjusting. The airport remains closed, schools have shifted to remote learning until Thursday, and Germany’s economy minister was seeking another route home. An international energy conference nevertheless opened as planned about 10 km from the airport. Whether the Saudi-Iranian contact produces restraint, or whether Washington joins the strikes, will likely shape the next phase for both the conflict and the oil risk premium. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Delivered crude prices surge back to highs as JPMorgan flags tanker crunch
item.description:
For oil, the note describes a market where the cost of delivery, rather than the barrel itself, is setting the marginal price. That can widen the gap between benchmark futures and what refiners actually pay, and it tends to reward freight exposure more directly than outright crude. Negative European refining margins raise the risk of run cuts, which would trim crude demand and could cap benchmark prices even while delivered costs stay high. Atlantic Basin grades moved on smaller ships carry higher per-barrel freight, a possible headwind for their competitiveness in distant markets.

---

Where we left off Friday:

  • investingLive Americas FX news wrap 9 Oct: It’s a Wrap: Stocks rebound despite weak sentiment; Canadian dollar falls on jobs miss

---

The oil market has found its April again, only this time the scarce commodity is the ship, not the crude.

Summary:

  • JPMorgan says delivered crude prices are back at spring highs and European refining margins have turned negative again, raising the risk of refinery run cuts
  • Unlike April’s crude shortage, the bank says October’s strain comes from the cost and difficulty of moving oil
  • Middle East flows through Hormuz rose from around 7.5 mbd in July and August to about 12 mbd in September, with more than four in five of the world’s VLCCs in use
  • Ship-to-ship transfers of up to 10 days and longer risk-avoiding routes are cutting how many cargoes each tanker can deliver
  • Around 125 Iranian VLCCs, roughly 13% of the global fleet, are largely unavailable to the mainstream market due to US measures
  • Middle East crude ex-Iran now needs about 35 more VLCCs, 13 Suezmaxes and 10 Aframaxes than the 2025 average, pushing demand onto smaller vessels worldwide

Oil markets are reliving the stress of April, but the cause has changed, according to a JPMorgan research note dated October 9. Delivered crude prices have climbed back to their spring peaks and European refining margins have slipped below zero again, raising the risk that refiners cut runs. Yet the bank argues the bottleneck this time is shipping capacity rather than a lack of crude.

The squeeze traces back to September, when Middle Eastern producers stepped up shipments through the Strait of Hormuz. Flows rose from roughly 7.5 million barrels per day across July and August to about 12 million in September, pulling a growing share of the tanker fleet into the region. By September, more than four in five of the world’s very large crude carriers, the biggest class of tanker, each able to carry around 2 million barrels, were in active service, leaving very little spare capacity.

JPMorgan says the issue is not only how many ships exist but how productively they are being used. More vessels are tied up in ship-to-ship transfers, where cargo is moved between tankers at sea, a process that can occupy a ship for up to 10 days. Others are taking longer routes to avoid higher-risk waters. Both lengthen voyages and reduce the number of cargoes each tanker can complete, so more ships are needed to move the same volume of oil.

Sanctions tighten the picture further. Around 125 Iranian VLCCs, equal to roughly 13% of the global fleet, are effectively shut out of the mainstream market by US measures, with many anchored or drifting in the Gulf or off Sri Lanka and Malaysia.

The bank estimates that moving Middle Eastern crude, excluding Iran, now requires an extra 35 VLCCs, 13 mid-sized Suezmaxes and 10 smaller Aframaxes compared with the 2025 average. As the region absorbs more of the fleet, VLCC employment elsewhere has fallen by 16 vessels.

Atlantic Basin producers are adapting by switching to smaller ships, with one VLCC cargo roughly equivalent to two Suezmaxes or three Aframaxes. Outside the Middle East, Aframax employment is up by about 140 vessels, or 23%, on the 2025 average, while Suezmax employment has risen by around 50 ships, or 11%. JPMorgan concludes that what started as a regional VLCC shortage has become a broad tightening across the global tanker fleet.

What makes this episode distinct is that more crude alone would not ease it: additional exports without additional ships could deepen the strain. The pace of Hormuz flows, rates for smaller tanker classes and any shift in US pressure on Iranian shipping are likely to decide whether this second April lasts as long as the first.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.
